intro: This unit tells the middle part of the Bible's story. The kingdom has split in two. Prophets stand up in the street and say things kings do not want to hear. Then two great empires come, one after the other. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria. The southern kingdom falls to Babylon, and the Temple burns. Many people are marched far from home.

But the story does not stop there. Far from home, people keep singing. They write psalms, collect wise sayings, ask hard questions and tell brave stories about Daniel and Esther. Then a new king, Cyrus of Persia, opens the door. The people walk home, rebuild the Temple, read the Torah out loud together and raise a wall.

By the end of this unit you will be able to say what a prophet is. You will know Elijah, Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and what each one said. You will put the years 722, 586 and 538 BCE in order. You will tell what kind of book Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Daniel and Esther each is. And you will explain how Jewish and Christian readers use these books today.
bigQuestion: How did a people keep their story alive through warning, loss and going home?

timeline.t: After Solomon, the kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Elijah faces King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
Amos the shepherd speaks in the northern kingdom about justice for the poor
Isaiah begins to speak in Jerusalem
Assyria captures Samaria; the northern kingdom of Israel ends
Babylon takes a first group of exiles, including Ezekiel
Babylon captures Jerusalem and burns the Temple; the exile begins
Cyrus lets the exiles return to Jerusalem
Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's wall; Ezra reads the Torah to the people

words.d: in the Bible, a person who speaks a message that the text says came from God
treating people fairly, especially the poor and the weak; a main theme of the prophets
the empire with its capital at Nineveh that captured Samaria in 722 BCE
the empire whose king Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem and burned the Temple in 586 BCE
being forced to live far from your homeland; the people of Judah were taken to Babylon
a name for Jerusalem, or for the hill the Temple stood on
something a prophet sees in the mind, like a dream while awake, that carries a message
a song or poem in the book of Psalms; there are 150 of them
a short saying that teaches a lesson about how to live
the spring holiday when Jews read the book of Esther, dress up and give gifts
the king of Persia who let the exiles return to Jerusalem in 538 BCE
the first five books of the Bible; the Hebrew word means teaching

test.q: In the Bible, a prophet is best described as what?
choices: A person who speaks a message to the people
A person who guards the Temple
A person who sees the future for money
test.why: A prophet is a messenger. The text says the message came from God and was spoken to kings and crowds.

test.q: Where did Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal take place?
test.why: 1 Kings 18 puts the contest on Mount Carmel, in the northern kingdom.

test.q: What did Elijah hear on Mount Horeb after the wind, earthquake and fire?
test.why: 1 Kings 19:12 says that after the fire came a still small voice.

test.q: Amos and Isaiah both said God cared most about what?
test.why: Amos 5 and Isaiah 1 both say justice for the poor, the orphan and the widow matters more than offerings.

choices: Cyrus let the exiles go home
test.why: Samaria fell in 722 BCE, the Temple burned in 586 BCE, Cyrus's order came in 538 BCE and the wall came later still.

test.q: Who wrote down Jeremiah's words, then wrote them again after the king burned them?
test.why: Jeremiah 36 says Baruch the scribe wrote the scroll and wrote it again after King Jehoiakim burned it.

test.q: What does the word exile mean?
choices: Being forced to live far from home
test.why: The exile was when the people of Judah were forced to live in Babylon, far from their land.

test.q: Psalm 137 says the people wept when they remembered what?
test.why: Psalm 137:1 says they sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept when they remembered Zion, which means Jerusalem.

test.q: In Ezekiel's vision, what happens to the dry bones?
test.why: Ezekiel 37 says the bones came together, were covered with skin, received breath and stood up.

test.q: Which book is the Bible's collection of 150 songs?
test.why: Psalms has 150 songs and poems for many feelings. Proverbs is wise sayings.

test.q: Which book asks why a good person suffers?
test.why: Job loses everything though he did nothing wrong, and the book asks why.

test.q: Why would Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego not bow to the statue?
choices: The king told them not to
They would worship only their own God
test.why: Daniel 3 says the three friends refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue and were thrown into the furnace.

test.q: How did Esther save her people?
choices: She went to the king uncalled and told him the truth
She prayed at an open window
test.why: Esther risked her life by going to the king without being called, then told him about Haman's plan.

test.q: What does the last book of the Tanakh, 2 Chronicles, end with?
choices: Cyrus letting the people go home
test.why: The Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's order to go up to Jerusalem. Christian Old Testaments end with Malachi instead.

test.q: What did Ezra do on the day described in Nehemiah 8?
choices: Rode around the wall at night
Read the Torah aloud to the whole people
Threw Haman's plan into the fire
test.why: Nehemiah 8 says Ezra read the law from morning to midday while helpers explained it to the people.

write.prompt: Pick this question: What did the prophets say would happen, and what gave the people hope after it did? Use two or three passages from this unit, such as Amos 5:24, 2 Kings 25, Psalm 137:1 or Ezekiel 37:1–14. For each one, say what the text says. Then tell how Jewish or Christian readers have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you use a passage.
Say who believes what: "Jewish tradition reads…" or "Many Christians read…", not "we believe."
Compare two readings instead of saying which one is right.
Use the unit's words: prophet, exile, justice, vision, Zion.

title: Prophets, Exile and Return

chapters.title: Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the Exile
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did the prophets say hard things, and what happened when nobody listened?

story.title: The Man at the Gate
story.kicker: A prophet stands at the city gate saying what nobody wants to hear.
paragraphs: The gate of Jerusalem is the busiest place in the city. Farmers push carts through it. Traders shout prices. Judges sit in the shade and settle arguments. On this morning a man stands in the middle of it all. His clothes are plain. His voice is loud. The book of Jeremiah says he stood at the Temple gate and spoke to everyone who came in.

"Stop cheating the stranger," he calls out. "Stop hurting the orphan and the widow. Do not think the Temple will keep you safe if you keep doing wrong." People frown. Some laugh. A priest tells him to be quiet. But the man keeps talking. He says the message is not his own. He says it comes from God.

The man's name is Jeremiah. The book that carries his name says he was told to speak when he was still young. He did not want the job. He said he could not talk well. But he went anyway, and he kept going for about forty years. Kings hated his message. One king cut up his scroll and burned it in a fire. Later Jeremiah was dropped into a muddy pit.

Jeremiah was not the first prophet, and he was not the last. Before him came Elijah, who faced a king on a mountain. Amos and Isaiah spoke up for the poor. After Jeremiah came Ezekiel, who spoke to people far from home. This chapter tells their stories in order, and it tells what happened to the two kingdoms they warned.

The story ends in a sad place: a burned Temple and a long walk to Babylon. But it does not end without hope. By the rivers of Babylon, the people wrote songs. And a prophet saw a valley of dry bones stand up and live.
story.think: Jeremiah kept speaking even when people laughed at him. Why do you think he did not stop?

lessons.title: A Message, Not a Fortune
lessons.mainIdea: In the Bible, a prophet is a person who speaks a message, most often to kings and crowds.
reading: The word *prophet* can sound like a fortune-teller. In the Bible it means something different. A prophet is a messenger. The text says God gives the prophet words, and the prophet says them out loud. Many prophets begin with the same line: "Thus says the LORD." That line tells the crowd whose message it is.

Prophets did not usually speak to quiet, friendly people. They spoke to kings, to priests and to crowds in the street. Often the message was hard to hear. It said: you are treating people badly, and trouble is coming unless you change. Sometimes the message was comfort: you are not forgotten.

Jewish tradition calls the second part of the Hebrew Bible the *Nevi'im*, which means Prophets. Christians read the same books in the Old Testament. Both count Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel as the three long books of prophets. Then come twelve shorter ones. In this chapter you will meet several of them.

words.d: in the Bible, a person who speaks a message that the text says came from God
the Hebrew word for Prophets; the second part of the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh

look.title: Two ways to hear one word
look.text: Two students hear the word prophet. One says, "That is someone who can see the future." The other says, "That is someone who brings a message people need to hear." Jeremiah stood at the Temple gate and told the crowd to stop cheating the stranger and hurting the orphan (Jeremiah 7). He was not reading the future. He was talking about that very day.
look.prompt: Which student is closer to what the Bible means by a prophet? What in Jeremiah's message tells you?

check.q: In the Bible, what does a prophet mainly do?
check.why: A prophet is a messenger. The text says the prophet speaks words that came from God, often to kings and crowds.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word Nevi'im mean?
check.why: Nevi'im means Prophets. It is the second part of the Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: Which line often begins a prophet's message?
check.why: Prophets often open with "Thus says the LORD" to show whose message they are bringing.

lessons.title: Elijah and the Fire on Carmel
lessons.mainIdea: The book of 1 Kings tells how Elijah faced King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
reading: Elijah lived in the northern kingdom, Israel, about 2,800 years ago. The king was Ahab. The book of 1 Kings says Ahab and his queen, Jezebel, worshiped a god named Baal. Elijah said there was only one God to worship. He told the king that no rain would fall until he said so. Then he hid.

After a long dry time, Elijah came back. He asked the king to meet him on Mount Carmel. 1 Kings 18 tells what happened. Elijah faced 450 prophets of Baal. Each side built an *altar* and laid wood on it. The rule was simple: whichever god sent fire from the sky was the real God.

The story says the prophets of Baal shouted all day, and nothing happened. Elijah even teased them. Then Elijah poured water on his own altar three times. He prayed one short prayer. The text says fire fell and burned up everything, even the water. The people fell down and said, "The LORD, he is God." Then the rain came.

words.d: a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel who faced King Ahab; his story is in 1 and 2 Kings
a raised place, often of stone, where people in the Bible burned offerings
a god worshiped by some of Israel's neighbors; the prophets said Israel must not worship him

look.title: One prayer on the mountain
look.text: The story says Elijah prayed something like this: "LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all this at your word." Then, the text says, fire fell from the sky.
look.cite: 1 Kings 18:36–38, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Elijah's prayer is short. What does he ask the people to learn from what happens next?

check.q: Where did Elijah face the prophets of Baal?
check.why: 1 Kings 18 sets the contest on Mount Carmel, in the northern kingdom of Israel.

check.q: Who was king of Israel in Elijah's story?
check.why: King Ahab and Queen Jezebel ruled Israel. David and Solomon lived earlier, and Cyrus was a king of Persia much later.

check.q: What did Elijah do to his altar before he prayed?
choices: He hid it in a cave
He carried it up the mountain
check.why: The story says Elijah poured water on the altar three times, so the fire that fell would be even more surprising.

lessons.title: The Still Small Voice
lessons.mainIdea: After the loud fire, 1 Kings 19 says Elijah heard God not in wind or earthquake but in a quiet voice.
reading: After the fire on Mount Carmel, Queen Jezebel was angry. She said she would kill Elijah. The bold prophet ran for his life. 1 Kings 19 says he went far south into the desert. He sat under a tree and said he wanted to give up. The story says an angel brought him bread and water. Then he walked forty days to a mountain called Horeb.

On the mountain, the text says, a great wind tore at the rocks. But God was not in the wind. Then the ground shook. But God was not in the earthquake. Then came a fire. But God was not in the fire. After the fire came something very quiet. The King James Version calls it "a still small voice."

Readers have loved this story for a long time. Some say it teaches that the biggest, loudest thing is not always the most important. Jewish and Christian readers both point out that Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where Moses met God. Elijah, the text says, went back to work after that quiet moment.

words.d: another name in the Bible for Mount Sinai, the mountain where Moses received the law
the King James Version's words for the quiet sound Elijah heard in 1 Kings 19

look.title: Not in the wind, not in the fire
look.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
look.prompt: The story lists three loud things and then one quiet thing. Why do you think the writer put them in that order?

check.q: Why did Elijah run away after Mount Carmel?
choices: Queen Jezebel said she would kill him
King Ahab made him a priest
check.why: 1 Kings 19 says Jezebel threatened Elijah's life, so he fled south into the desert.

check.q: In the story, where was God found on Mount Horeb?
check.why: The text says God was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in a still small voice.

check.q: Horeb is another name for which mountain?
check.why: The Bible uses Horeb and Sinai for the same mountain, where Moses received the law.

lessons.title: Amos the Shepherd
lessons.mainIdea: Amos, a shepherd, told the rich people of Israel that God cared how they treated the poor.
reading: Amos was not a priest or a prince. His book says he was a shepherd from a small town called Tekoa. He lived about 760 BCE, around the time of Elijah's great-grandchildren. The northern kingdom, Israel, was rich then. The book of Amos says the rich lived in fancy houses while the poor were sold for the price of a pair of shoes.

Amos walked north and spoke in the town of Bethel. His message was sharp. He said God did not want fancy songs and big festivals from people who cheated the poor. He said that *justice* should flow like a river that never dries up. A priest named Amaziah told Amos to go home. Amos said he was only saying what he was sent to say.

Amos is the first of the Twelve, the shorter books of prophets. His words are short, strong and often like poems. Jewish and Christian readers still quote Amos when they talk about fairness. In 1963, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. used a line from Amos in his most famous speech in Washington.

words.d: a shepherd from Tekoa who spoke in the northern kingdom about 760 BCE; his book is one of the Twelve
treating people fairly, especially the poor and the weak; a main theme of the prophets

look.title: Like a river
look.text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
look.prompt: Amos compares fairness to a river. A river keeps moving and never stops. What does that picture say about how fairness should work?

check.q: What was Amos's job before he spoke as a prophet?
check.why: The book of Amos says he was a shepherd from Tekoa, not a priest or a prince.

check.q: What was the main point of Amos's message?
check.why: Amos said God cared more about justice for the poor than about festivals and songs.

check.q: Amos compares justice to what?
choices: A river that never dries up
check.why: Amos 5:24 asks that justice roll down like water and fairness like a strong stream.

lessons.title: Isaiah in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah spoke in Jerusalem and said that caring for the orphan and the widow mattered more than offerings.
reading: Isaiah lived in Jerusalem, the capital of the southern kingdom, Judah. He spoke about 740 to 700 BCE, a little after Amos. The book of Isaiah says he saw a vision in the Temple. He saw God on a high throne, and he felt small and unclean. The text says a burning coal touched his lips, and then he was ready to speak.

Like Amos, Isaiah said that fairness came first. In the very first chapter of his book, he tells people to stop doing evil and learn to do good. He tells them to help the *orphan* and speak up for the *widow*. In that time, a child with no father and a woman with no husband had no one to protect them. Isaiah said God would.

Isaiah also spoke to kings about war. The great empire of Assyria was growing. Isaiah told King Hezekiah not to panic and not to trust in Egypt's army. The book of Isaiah is long, with 66 chapters. Many scholars think later writers added to it during and after the exile. Jews and Christians both read Isaiah, and sometimes read the same verses in different ways.

words.d: a prophet in Jerusalem, about 740 to 700 BCE; his book is the longest book of the prophets
a child whose parents have died; the prophets said such children must be protected
a woman whose husband has died; in Bible times she often had no one to care for her

look.title: Learn to do good
look.text: The book of Isaiah says, in simple words: Stop doing evil. Learn to do good. Look for what is fair. Help the person who is being crushed. Stand up for the orphan. Speak for the widow.
look.cite: Isaiah 1:16–17, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Isaiah names two groups of people to protect. Why do you think he picked those two?

check.q: In which city did Isaiah speak?
check.why: Isaiah lived and spoke in Jerusalem, the capital of the southern kingdom of Judah.

check.q: Which two groups does Isaiah 1 say to protect?
check.why: Isaiah 1:17 tells the people to stand up for the orphan and speak for the widow.

check.q: What does the book of Isaiah say happened when he was called?
choices: He heard a still small voice
check.why: Isaiah 6 tells of a vision in the Temple where a burning coal touched Isaiah's lips. The bush is Moses's story and the voice is Elijah's.

lessons.title: How Prophets Spoke
lessons.mainIdea: Prophets used poems, pictures and even actions to make their message hard to forget.
reading: Prophets wanted people to remember. So they did not talk in a flat voice. Much of their message is *poetry*. Hebrew poems say a thing, then say it again in a new way. Amos said justice should roll like water, then said fairness should flow like a stream. Two lines, one idea. That helps the words stick.

Prophets also used pictures in words. Isaiah said sins as red as blood could become white as snow. Jeremiah watched a potter shape wet clay and said God could reshape a people the same way. These pictures came from everyday life: farms, kitchens, city gates and markets.

Sometimes a prophet acted out the message. This is called a sign-act. Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke, the kind put on an ox, to show that Babylon would rule over Judah. Ezekiel lay on his side for many days to stand for the years of wrongdoing. People might forget a speech, but they would not forget a man wearing a yoke.

words.d: writing with rhythm and pictures; Hebrew poetry often says one idea in two matching lines
an action a prophet did in public to show a message, like Jeremiah wearing a yoke

look.title: Say it twice
look.text: Read these two lines from the prophet Micah, retold in simple words: "They will beat their swords into plows, and their spears into tools for pruning trees." (Micah 4:3) A sword and a spear are for fighting. A plow and a pruning tool are for growing food. The second line says the same idea as the first, with a new picture.
look.prompt: What is the one idea both lines share? Try writing your own two lines that say one idea two ways.

check.q: How does Hebrew poetry often work?
choices: It says one idea in two matching lines
It is always exactly ten lines
check.why: Hebrew poetry says a thing, then says it again a new way. Amos 5:24 is an example.

check.q: What is a sign-act?
choices: A song sung in the Temple
An action a prophet did to show a message
A letter sent to a king
check.why: A sign-act is a public action, like Jeremiah wearing a yoke, that shows the prophet's message.

check.q: Which prophet watched a potter shape clay?
check.why: Jeremiah 18 tells of Jeremiah watching a potter and using it as a picture of how a people can be reshaped.

lessons.title: Assyria Takes Israel
lessons.mainIdea: In 722 BCE the empire of Assyria captured Samaria, and the northern kingdom of Israel came to an end.
reading: After King Solomon died, the kingdom had split in two. The north was called Israel, with its capital at Samaria. The south was called Judah, with its capital at Jerusalem. The prophets Amos and Hosea had warned the north. The book of 2 Kings says most of its kings did what was wrong.

To the northeast lay a huge empire called *Assyria*. Its capital was Nineveh. Assyria had a strong army and a habit of moving whole peoples from one land to another. In 722 BCE, the Assyrian army captured Samaria. 2 Kings 17 says many people of Israel were carried away to far cities. Others were brought in to take their place.

The northern kingdom never came back. Later people spoke of the "lost tribes" of Israel. Judah, in the south, was still standing. Twenty years later Assyria came for Jerusalem too. The book of 2 Kings and the book of Isaiah both say the city was surrounded but not taken. Judah had a little more time.

words.d: a powerful empire with its capital at Nineveh; it captured Samaria in 722 BCE
the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel
the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem as its capital, after the kingdom split in two

look.title: Two kingdoms, two endings
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians; 2 Kings 17 and 25
look.prompt: Years BCE count down. How many years passed between the fall of Samaria and the fall of Jerusalem?

check.q: What was the capital of the northern kingdom, Israel?
check.why: Samaria was Israel's capital. Jerusalem was Judah's, Nineveh was Assyria's and Babylon was Babylon's.

check.q: In what year did Assyria capture Samaria?
check.why: Historians date the fall of Samaria to 722 BCE. The other years are the split of the kingdom, the fall of Jerusalem and the return.

check.q: What did Assyria often do to the peoples it conquered?
check.why: 2 Kings 17 says Assyria carried away the people of Israel and brought in others, which was a common Assyrian practice.

lessons.title: Jeremiah Warns Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Jeremiah told Jerusalem that Babylon would come, and the city's leaders tried hard to make him stop.
reading: About a hundred years after Samaria fell, a new empire rose: Babylon. Its king was Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah lived in Judah then. His book says he began speaking when he was young, in the days of good King Josiah. Josiah had found a book of the law in the Temple and led the people back to it. But Josiah died in battle, and the kings after him did not listen.

Jeremiah said Babylon was coming and that fighting it would not work. Nobody wanted to hear it. Jeremiah 36 says he spoke his words to a *scribe* named Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll. King Jehoiakim had the scroll read to him. He cut off each piece and threw it in the fire. Jeremiah simply had Baruch write it all again, with more added.

Later, Jeremiah 38 says, the leaders dropped him into an empty water pit. He sank in the mud. A servant from Africa named Ebed-melech pulled him out with ropes and old rags. Jeremiah is sometimes called the weeping prophet. His book has anger in it, but also great sadness for his city.

words.d: a prophet in Judah who warned Jerusalem before Babylon came; his book carries his name
a person whose job was writing and copying; Baruch was Jeremiah's scribe
a great city and empire on the Euphrates River; its king Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem

look.title: The scroll in the fire
look.text: Picture a winter room with a fire pot burning. A reader unrolls a scroll and reads a few columns. The king takes a knife, cuts off what was read, and drops it into the fire. He does this until the whole scroll is gone. Some men beg him to stop. He does not. Across the city, a prophet hears the news and tells his scribe to get a new scroll (Jeremiah 36).
look.prompt: The king thought burning the scroll would end the message. Did it? What does the story say happened next?

check.q: Who wrote down Jeremiah's words on a scroll?
check.why: Jeremiah 36 says the scribe Baruch wrote the words Jeremiah spoke.

check.q: What did King Jehoiakim do with Jeremiah's scroll?
choices: Read it to the whole city
check.why: Jeremiah 36 says the king cut the scroll and burned it in the fire, and Jeremiah had it written again.

check.q: Which empire did Jeremiah say was coming?
check.why: Jeremiah warned that Babylon, under King Nebuchadnezzar, would take Jerusalem. Assyria had fallen by then.

lessons.title: The Temple Burns
lessons.mainIdea: In 586 BCE Babylon captured Jerusalem, burned the Temple and took many people into exile.
reading: 2 Kings 25 tells the end of the kingdom of Judah in plain words. The army of Babylon surrounded Jerusalem. Food ran out. The wall was broken. The last king, Zedekiah, tried to escape at night and was caught. Then a Babylonian officer burned the Temple that Solomon had built, the king's palace and every big house in the city.

This happened in 586 BCE. Many people were marched away to Babylon, hundreds of miles to the east. This is called the *exile*. A first group had been taken about ten years earlier, and Ezekiel was among them. The poorest people were left behind to work the land. Jeremiah stayed with them for a time.

The book of Lamentations is a set of sad poems about the fallen city. Jewish tradition reads it aloud each year on the day called Tisha B'Av, which remembers the Temple's fall. Christians read it too. For both, this was the hardest moment in the Bible's history story so far. The prophets had said it would come. Now it had.

words.d: being forced to live far from your homeland; the people of Judah were taken to Babylon in 586 BCE
a short book of sad poems about the fall of Jerusalem
a day of fasting when Jews remember the burning of the Temple

look.title: What 2 Kings says happened
look.text: 2 Kings 25 says, in simple words: The captain of the Babylonian guard came to Jerusalem. He burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and all the houses of the city. His army broke down the walls. The people who were left were carried away, except for some of the poorest, who stayed to farm the land.
look.cite: 2 Kings 25:8–12, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The writer lists what was burned and who was taken. Why do you think the writer gives these facts without adding feelings?

check.q: In what year did Babylon capture Jerusalem and burn the Temple?
check.why: 2 Kings 25 tells of the fall of Jerusalem, which historians date to 586 BCE.

check.q: What does the word exile mean?
choices: Being forced to live far from home
check.why: The exile was when the people of Judah were forced to live in Babylon, far from their land.

check.q: Which book is a set of sad poems about the fallen city?
check.why: Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem. Jewish tradition reads it on Tisha B'Av.

lessons.title: By the Rivers of Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 137 is a song from the exile about missing Jerusalem and not being able to sing.
reading: Babylon was a great city with wide walls and gardens. But to the people from Judah it was a strange place. They had lost their homes, their Temple and their king. Psalm 137 gives their feelings a voice. It says they sat by the rivers of Babylon and cried when they remembered *Zion*, which is a name for Jerusalem.

The psalm says their captors asked them to sing one of the songs of Zion. The people answered with a question: how can we sing the LORD's song in a strange land? They hung their harps on the willow trees. Then the singer makes a promise never to forget Jerusalem.

Psalm 137 ends with angry words against Babylon. Jewish and Christian readers have handled that ending in different ways. Some skip it in worship. Others say it shows how honest the psalms are about pain. Either way, the psalm shows that the exiles did not lose their story. They kept writing and singing.

words.d: a name for Jerusalem, or for the hill the Temple stood on
a song or poem in the book of Psalms; Psalm 137 comes from the exile

look.title: We sat down and wept
look.text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
look.prompt: The singer says "we" and not "I." What does that tell you about who this song was for?

check.q: Zion is another name for what?
check.why: Zion means Jerusalem, or the hill where the Temple stood.

check.q: In Psalm 137, what did the exiles hang on the willow trees?
check.why: The psalm says they hung up their harps because they could not sing in a strange land.

check.q: Why does Psalm 137 matter for understanding the exile?
choices: It lists the laws of Babylon
It tells how the Temple was built
It names every king of Judah
It shows the exiles' feelings in a song
check.why: Psalm 137 gives the exiles a voice. It shows their sadness and their promise not to forget Jerusalem.

lessons.title: Ezekiel and the Dry Bones
lessons.mainIdea: In Babylon, Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones come to life, a picture of hope for a people who felt finished.
reading: Ezekiel was a priest. He was taken to Babylon in the first group, before the Temple fell. His book says he lived by a river called Chebar with other exiles. There, the text says, he saw strange and powerful visions. He saw wheels full of eyes. He saw a scroll he had to eat. He saw a new Temple, measured room by room.

His most famous vision is in Ezekiel 37. The text says he was set down in a valley full of dry bones. A voice asked him, "Can these bones live?" Ezekiel said only God knew. He was told to speak to the bones. As he spoke, the bones rattled and came together. Skin covered them. Then breath came, and a huge crowd stood up.

The text explains the picture. The bones are the people of Israel, who said, "Our hope is lost." The *vision* says they will live again and go home. Jewish readers have read this as a promise to the whole people. Many Christians read it that way too. Some also read it as a picture of new life after death. It is a message of hope in the darkest part of the story.

words.d: a priest and prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon; his book is full of visions
something a prophet sees in the mind, like a dream while awake, that carries a message
believing that good can still come, even when things look finished

look.title: Can these bones live?
look.text: Ezekiel 37 says, in simple words: The hand of the LORD set me down in a valley full of bones, and they were very dry. He asked me, "Can these bones live?" I said, "O Lord GOD, you know." He said, "Speak to these bones: O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD."
look.cite: Ezekiel 37:1–4, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Ezekiel does not answer yes or no. Why might the writer have him answer that way?

check.q: Where did Ezekiel live when he had his visions?
check.why: Ezekiel was taken to Babylon in the first group and lived by the river Chebar with other exiles.

check.q: In Ezekiel 37, what do the dry bones stand for?
check.why: The text says the bones are the whole house of Israel, who felt their hope was lost.

check.q: What is the main message of the dry bones vision?
choices: Hope: the people will live again
Do not sing in a strange land
check.why: The vision says a people who felt finished will stand up and live. It is a message of hope in exile.

review.q: What does a prophet do in the Bible?
choices: Speaks a message, often to kings and crowds
review.why: A prophet is a messenger. The text says the message came from God and was spoken to the people.

review.q: On Mount Carmel, what did the story say showed which god was real?
review.why: 1 Kings 18 says the god who answered with fire was the true God, and fire fell on Elijah's altar.

review.q: Which prophet was a shepherd from Tekoa?
review.why: The book of Amos says Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa who spoke in the northern kingdom.

review.q: Which empire captured Samaria in 722 BCE?
review.why: Assyria took Samaria in 722 BCE. Babylon took Jerusalem later, in 586 BCE.

review.q: What did King Jehoiakim do to Jeremiah's scroll?
review.why: Jeremiah 36 says the king cut the scroll into pieces and burned it.

choices: Cyrus let the exiles go home
review.why: 2 Kings 25 tells of Babylon capturing Jerusalem and burning the Temple, dated to 586 BCE.
Psalm 137 says the people wept by the rivers of Babylon when they remembered Zion.

review.q: How do Jewish readers most often read Ezekiel's dry bones?
choices: As a promise that the whole people will live again
As a song for the Temple
review.why: Ezekiel 37 says the bones are the house of Israel, and Jewish tradition reads it as hope for the people's return.

chapters.title: Psalms, Proverbs, Daniel, Esther and Home Again
chapters.bigQuestion: How did songs, wise sayings and brave stories help a people keep going, and what did going home look like?

story.title: The Queen Who Spoke
story.kicker: A queen who was told to stay quiet decides to speak.
paragraphs: Esther is the queen of Persia, the largest empire in the world. She lives in a palace in the city of Susa. But she has a secret. She is Jewish, and nobody in the palace knows it. Her cousin Mordecai, who raised her, told her to keep quiet about it. So far, she has.

Now a man named Haman has a plan. He is the king's top helper, and he hates Mordecai, because Mordecai will not bow to him. Haman gets the king to sign an order. On one day, every Jewish person in the empire will be killed. The order goes out to every province. Mordecai tears his clothes and sits in the street in sackcloth.

Mordecai sends Esther a message: go to the king and beg for your people. Esther sends one back. Nobody may go to the king without being called. Anyone who does can be put to death. And the king has not called her for thirty days.

Mordecai answers with the most famous line in the book. Do not think you will be safe in the palace, he says. And who knows? Maybe you became queen for a time just like this. Esther reads the message. She asks all the Jews in Susa to fast with her for three days. Then she says the words that turn the story: "If I die, I die."

On the third day she puts on her royal robes and walks into the king's court. He holds out his golden scepter. She may speak. This chapter is about the books of the Bible that Jewish tradition calls the Writings: songs, wise sayings, hard questions and brave stories like Esther's. It ends with the people going home.
story.think: Esther had to choose between staying safe and speaking up. What made her decide to speak?

lessons.title: Psalm 23: The Shepherd
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd who leads, feeds and protects, and it is loved by Jews and Christians alike.
reading: The book of *Psalms* is the Bible's songbook. It has 150 songs. Some are happy, some are sad, some are angry, and some are quiet. Jewish tradition puts Psalms in the third part of the Tanakh, the Writings, called *Ketuvim* in Hebrew. Many psalms carry the name of King David at the top, and tradition remembers David as a singer and harp player.

Psalm 23 is the most famous psalm of all. It is short, just six verses. It begins by saying the LORD is the singer's *shepherd*. A shepherd leads sheep to green grass and still water. The psalm says the singer will not be in need. Even in a dark valley, the singer says, I will not be afraid, because you are with me.

Then the picture changes. The singer is at a table, a guest at a feast, with a full cup. The psalm ends with the hope of living in the house of the LORD forever. Jews say this psalm at some meals and at funerals. Christians read it at funerals and in church. People who have never opened a Bible often know its first line.

words.d: the Bible's book of 150 songs and poems; in Hebrew, Tehillim, which means praises
the Hebrew word for Writings; the third part of the Tanakh, which includes Psalms
a person who cares for sheep; Psalm 23 uses it as a picture of God

look.title: The first line
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
look.prompt: Here "want" means to be in need. What does a shepherd give sheep that they would otherwise lack?

check.q: How many psalms are in the book of Psalms?
check.why: The book of Psalms has 150 songs. Sixty-six is the number of books in most Protestant Bibles.

check.q: What picture of God does Psalm 23 begin with?
check.why: Psalm 23:1 says "The LORD is my shepherd," and the whole psalm follows that picture.

check.q: In which part of the Tanakh are the Psalms?
check.why: Jewish tradition places Psalms among the Ketuvim, the Writings. The Gospels are in the New Testament.

lessons.title: Psalm 100 and Psalm 150: Praise
lessons.mainIdea: Psalms 100 and 150 are songs of praise that call for joy, music and every living thing to join in.
reading: Not every psalm is quiet like Psalm 23. Many are loud. Psalm 100 tells all the earth to make a joyful noise. It tells people to come into God's gates with thanks. In simple words it says: know that the LORD is God, he made us, we are his people and his sheep. It is only five verses long, and it is sung in synagogues and churches to this day.

Psalm 150 is the last psalm in the book. It is like a grand finish. Every line begins with the word *praise*. It names the instruments: trumpet, harp, drum, strings, flute, loud cymbals. It sounds like a band playing all at once. Its last line says that everything that breathes should praise the LORD.

Psalms like these are called praise psalms. Others are called *laments*, sad songs that cry out for help, like Psalm 137. Some psalms give thanks. Some are for a king's coronation. Some were sung on the walk up to Jerusalem for a festival. The book has a song for almost every feeling a person can have.

words.d: to speak or sing about how good someone is; praise psalms sing about God
a sad song that cries out in pain and asks for help

look.title: The last line of the book
look.text: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
look.prompt: This is the last verse of the whole book of Psalms. Why is it a good line to end on?

check.q: What does Psalm 100 tell all the earth to do?
check.why: Psalm 100 opens by calling all lands to make a joyful noise and to come with thanks.

check.q: What is a lament?
choices: A sad song that asks for help
check.why: A lament is a sad song. Psalm 137, sung in exile, is a lament.

check.q: Which psalm names trumpets, harps, drums and cymbals?
check.why: Psalm 150, the last psalm, calls for praise with a long list of instruments.

lessons.title: Five Books of Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The 150 psalms are grouped into five smaller books, each ending with a line of blessing.
reading: If you open the book of Psalms, you will see it is split into five parts. Book One runs from Psalm 1 to Psalm 41. Book Two goes to Psalm 72. Book Three ends at Psalm 89, Book Four at Psalm 106 and Book Five at Psalm 150. Each book ends with a short blessing, often with the word *amen*, which means "truly" or "so be it."

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have noticed something. Five is also the number of books in the Torah. Old Jewish teaching says the five books of Psalms match the five books of Moses. Whether or not that was the plan, the shape helps. It shows the book was put together with care. It grew over a long time, from many singers.

Not all psalms are by David. Some name other singers, like Asaph or the sons of Korah. Some name no one. Psalm 90 is called a prayer of Moses. Some psalms were clearly written in the exile or after it. So the book of Psalms grew the way a hymnbook grows, with new songs added as the years went on.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning truly or so be it, said at the end of a prayer or blessing
a collection of songs for worship; the book of Psalms is like an ancient hymnbook

look.title: Where each book of Psalms ends
look.cite: The book of Psalms, as divided in the Hebrew Bible and in the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Which of the five books has the most psalms? Count them from the numbers.

check.q: Into how many smaller books is the book of Psalms divided?
check.why: Psalms has five books, ending at Psalms 41, 72, 89, 106 and 150.

check.q: What does the word amen mean?
check.why: Amen is a Hebrew word meaning truly or so be it. Each book of Psalms ends with a blessing and amen.

check.q: Which is true about who wrote the psalms?
choices: Some name David, some name others, some name no one
check.why: Many psalms carry David's name, but others name Asaph, the sons of Korah or Moses, and some name nobody.

lessons.title: Proverbs: Short and Wise
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Proverbs is a collection of short sayings about how to live wisely.
reading: A *proverb* is a short saying that packs a lot of wisdom into a few words. "Look before you leap" is an English proverb. The Bible has a whole book of them, 31 chapters long. The book of Proverbs names King Solomon at its start. Tradition remembers Solomon as the wisest king. Some parts of the book name other wise teachers too.

Most proverbs come in two lines. Often the second line is the opposite of the first. One says a soft answer turns anger away, but harsh words stir it up. Another says a wise child makes a father glad, but a foolish one makes a mother sad. The two lines make you think about the choice.

The first chapters of Proverbs are like a parent talking to a child. Listen. Be careful about friends. Work hard. Do not be like the lazy person who will not get out of bed. The book says the start of *wisdom* is respect for the LORD. The last chapter praises a strong, wise woman. She runs her house and helps the poor. Jewish families sing that poem on Friday nights.

words.d: a short saying that teaches a lesson about how to live
knowing how to live well and make good choices; the subject of Proverbs
David's son and the king remembered for his wisdom; Proverbs names him at its start

look.title: A soft answer
look.text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
look.prompt: Wrath means anger. Grievous means harsh. Tell about a time when a soft answer calmed someone down.

check.q: What is a proverb?
check.why: A proverb is a short saying that teaches a lesson. The book of Proverbs is full of them.

check.q: Which king does the book of Proverbs name at its start?
check.why: Proverbs opens by naming Solomon, the king tradition remembers as the wisest.

check.q: How are many proverbs built?
choices: As a question and a riddle
check.why: Most proverbs have two lines, and often the second says the opposite of the first, like the soft answer and the harsh word.

lessons.title: Job's Hard Question
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Job asks why good people suffer, and it does not give an easy answer.
reading: The book of Job begins with a good man who has everything: a big family, many animals, good health. Then, in one terrible day, he loses it all. His animals are stolen. A storm kills his children. Then he gets painful sores from head to foot. Job sits in the ashes. He did nothing wrong. So he asks: why?

Three friends come to sit with him. At first they say nothing for seven days. Then they start to talk, and they say the wrong things. They say Job must have done something bad, because bad things only happen to bad people. Job says that is not true. He wants to ask God himself. Most of the book is this long argument, written as poetry.

At the end, the text says God speaks to Job out of a storm. God does not explain why Job suffered. Instead God asks questions: where were you when I made the earth? Can you make it rain? Job says he is too small to understand. Then the text says God gives Job a new family and new health. Jewish and Christian readers have argued for a very long time about what the book means. Many say its point is that the question is real and honest.

words.d: a good man in the book of Job who loses everything and asks God why
to go through pain or loss
a storm of spinning wind; the book of Job says God spoke to Job out of one

look.title: The friends who said the wrong things
look.text: Job's friend Eliphaz says, in simple words: "Think about it. Who was ever punished when he was innocent? People who plant trouble harvest trouble." (Job 4:7–8) Job answers that he is innocent and that he is suffering anyway. He tells his friends they would be wiser if they stayed silent (Job 13:5).
look.prompt: Eliphaz thinks bad things only happen to bad people. What does Job's own story say about that idea?

check.q: What is the big question of the book of Job?
check.why: Job loses everything though he did nothing wrong, and the book asks why.

check.q: What did Job's three friends say?
choices: That Job should move to Egypt
That Job must have done something bad
That God would give Job a new family
check.why: The friends say suffering only comes to the guilty. Job says that is not true of him.

check.q: How does the text say God answered Job?
choices: With a list of Job's sins
check.why: Job 38 says God spoke out of the whirlwind and asked Job questions about the making of the world.

lessons.title: Daniel and His Friends
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Daniel tells of young exiles in Babylon who kept their ways and were kept safe in a furnace and a lions' den.
reading: The book of Daniel is set in Babylon during the exile. It says Daniel and three friends were taken from Judah as boys and trained to serve the king. They were given new names: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Daniel 1 says they would not eat the king's rich food. They asked for vegetables and water for ten days, and they ended up healthier than the others.

Daniel 3 tells of a huge golden statue. King Nebuchadnezzar ordered everyone to bow to it when the music played. The three friends would not bow. The king had them thrown into a *furnace* so hot it killed the guards. The story says the king looked in and saw four men walking in the fire, not three. The friends came out without even the smell of smoke.

In Daniel 6, a later king, Darius, is tricked into making a law: pray to no one but the king for thirty days. Daniel keeps praying at his window, three times a day, as he always did. He is thrown into a *den* of lions. The story says the king could not sleep. In the morning, Daniel was alive. The text says an angel shut the lions' mouths. Jewish and Christian readers tell these as stories of courage.

words.d: a young exile in Babylon whose book tells of the furnace, the lions' den and visions
a very hot oven; Daniel 3 says three friends were thrown into one and came out unhurt
the home of a wild animal; Daniel 6 says Daniel was put into a den of lions

look.title: The window that stayed open
look.text: Picture a house in Babylon. An upstairs window faces west, toward Jerusalem, hundreds of miles away. Three times a day a man kneels there and prays, and everyone can see him. A new law says praying to anyone but the king is a crime. The man hears about the law. He goes upstairs, opens the window, and kneels as he always has (Daniel 6:10).
look.prompt: Daniel could have prayed in secret. Why do you think the story has him keep the window open?

check.q: What did Daniel and his friends ask to eat instead of the king's food?
check.why: Daniel 1 says they asked for vegetables and water for ten days and came out healthier.

check.q: Why were Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego thrown into the furnace?
choices: They would not bow to the golden statue
check.why: Daniel 3 says the three friends refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue when the music played.

check.q: Which king's law put Daniel in the lions' den?
check.why: Daniel 6 names King Darius, who was tricked into a law against praying to anyone but the king.

lessons.title: Esther Speaks Up
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Esther tells how a Jewish queen in Persia risked her life to save her people, remembered each year at Purim.
reading: The book of Esther takes place in Persia, the empire that came after Babylon. The king is called Ahasuerus. Esther, a Jewish girl raised by her cousin Mordecai, becomes his queen. She keeps her people a secret. Then Haman, the king's top helper, plans to kill all the Jews in the empire on one day, chosen by casting lots. The Hebrew word for lots is *pur*.

Mordecai begs Esther to go to the king. She knows she could die for going uncalled. But she goes. At a dinner she tells the king the truth: she is Jewish, and Haman's plan will kill her too. The king is furious with Haman. Haman ends up on the very gallows he built for Mordecai. The Jews are allowed to defend themselves, and they are saved.

Jews remember this story every spring at the holiday of *Purim*. In the synagogue the whole book is read aloud from a scroll called the *Megillah*. Every time Haman's name is read, people shake noisemakers and stamp their feet to drown it out. Children dress in costumes. Families give food to friends and gifts to the poor. Esther is one of two books in the Bible named for a woman. The other is Ruth.

words.d: a Jewish queen of Persia whose book tells how she saved her people
the spring holiday when Jews read the book of Esther, dress up and give gifts
the Hebrew word for scroll; the scroll of Esther read at Purim

look.title: For such a time as this
look.text: Mordecai's message to Esther ends with these words: "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
look.prompt: Mordecai asks a question instead of giving an order. Why might a question work better here?

check.q: In which empire does the book of Esther take place?
check.why: Esther is set in Persia, under King Ahasuerus, after the fall of Babylon.

check.q: Who planned to kill all the Jews in the empire?
check.why: Haman, the king's top helper, made the plan because Mordecai would not bow to him.

check.q: What do people do at Purim when Haman's name is read?
choices: Make noise to drown it out
check.why: At the Megillah reading, people shake noisemakers and stamp when they hear Haman's name.

lessons.title: Cyrus Opens the Door
lessons.mainIdea: In 538 BCE, Cyrus of Persia let the exiles return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple.
reading: Babylon did not last forever. In 539 BCE a new empire, Persia, took the city. Its king was *Cyrus*. Persia ruled differently from Babylon. The book of Ezra says that in his first year over Babylon, Cyrus sent out an order. Any of the people of Judah who wished could go home to Jerusalem and build a house for their God. He even gave back the Temple's gold and silver cups.

Not everyone went. Some families had lived in Babylon for fifty years, and it was home now. But the book of Ezra says about 42,000 people made the long trip back. They found Jerusalem in ruins. They built an altar first, then began the Temple. Neighbors tried to stop them. The work stopped and started. The second Temple was finished about 515 BCE.

Cyrus's order is important for another reason. In the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh, the last book is 2 Chronicles. Its very last verses tell of Cyrus letting the people go up to Jerusalem. So the Hebrew Bible ends with going home. Christian Old Testaments put the books in a different order and end with the prophet Malachi. The same books, ordered two ways, end on two different notes.

words.d: the king of Persia who let the exiles of Judah return to Jerusalem in 538 BCE
the empire that captured Babylon in 539 BCE; today the land of Iran
going back; the return from exile began under Cyrus

look.title: From exile to home
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians; 2 Kings 25, Ezra 1 and 6, Nehemiah 2 and 6
look.prompt: About how many years were the people in exile before Cyrus let them go home?

check.q: Which empire captured Babylon in 539 BCE?
check.why: Persia, under Cyrus, took Babylon in 539 BCE. Assyria had fallen long before.

check.q: What did Cyrus's order allow?
choices: Exiles to return and rebuild the Temple
The Torah to be written in Persian
check.why: Ezra 1 says Cyrus let the people of Judah go home to Jerusalem and build a house for their God.

check.q: Which book ends the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh?
check.why: The Tanakh ends with 2 Chronicles and Cyrus's order to go home. Christian Old Testaments end with Malachi.

lessons.title: Ezra Reads the Torah
lessons.mainIdea: Nehemiah 8 tells of Ezra reading the Torah aloud to the whole people, who listened from morning to midday.
reading: Ezra was a priest and a *scribe*. A scribe was trained to copy and explain the law. The book of Ezra says he came from Babylon to Jerusalem after the Temple was rebuilt. He brought scrolls of the *Torah*, the teaching given through Moses. His job was to teach it to a people who had grown up far from home.

Nehemiah 8 tells of a special day. All the people gathered in a square by the Water Gate. Ezra stood on a wooden platform. He opened the scroll, and everyone stood up. He read from early morning until midday. Helpers walked among the crowd and explained the words so that everyone understood. Men, women and children old enough to understand were all there.

The text says the people cried when they heard the words. Ezra and Nehemiah told them not to cry. This day was holy, they said. Go eat good food, drink sweet drinks, and share with anyone who has nothing. Then the people built leafy huts and kept the festival of Sukkot, as the Torah told them. Jewish readers see this day as a new beginning. Reading the Torah out loud is still the center of a synagogue service.

words.d: a priest and scribe who brought the Torah from Babylon and read it aloud in Jerusalem
a person trained to copy, read and explain the law
the first five books of the Bible; the Hebrew word means teaching

look.title: A day for reading out loud
look.text: Nehemiah 8 says, in simple words: Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform above the people. He opened the book, and all the people stood up. He read from morning until midday, and the ears of the people were on the book of the law. The helpers read clearly and gave the meaning, so the people understood.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:1–8, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: The text says helpers explained the words. Why was explaining as important as reading?

check.q: What was Ezra's job?
check.why: Ezra was a priest and scribe, trained to read, copy and explain the Torah.

check.q: Where did Ezra read the Torah aloud?
choices: In a square by the Water Gate in Jerusalem
check.why: Nehemiah 8 sets the reading in the square before the Water Gate in Jerusalem.

check.q: What did Ezra and Nehemiah tell the crying people to do?
choices: Eat, drink and share with those who had nothing
check.why: The text says the day was holy, so the people should celebrate and send food to anyone in need.

lessons.title: Nehemiah Builds the Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Nehemiah left a palace job in Persia to rebuild Jerusalem's broken wall, and the book says it took 52 days.
reading: Nehemiah had a good job in Persia. He was the king's *cupbearer*, the trusted servant who tasted the wine and stood beside the throne. But his book says he heard news from Jerusalem: the wall was still broken, and the gates were burned. He sat down and cried. Then he prayed, and he asked the king for leave to go and rebuild.

The king said yes and gave him letters and wood. Nehemiah rode to Jerusalem. On his first night he went out in secret and rode around the broken wall to see how bad it was. Then he called the people together. Nehemiah 3 lists family after family, each building the part of the wall near its own house. Priests, goldsmiths, perfume makers and their daughters all worked.

Enemies laughed at them and then threatened to attack. So the builders worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. Nehemiah 6 says the wall was finished in 52 days. The people then gathered for Ezra's great reading of the Torah. The books of Ezra and Nehemiah close the Bible's history of the return. The people were home, with a Temple, a wall and the Torah.

words.d: the king of Persia's cupbearer who went to Jerusalem and led the rebuilding of the wall
a trusted servant who served the king's wine and stood near the throne

look.title: Each family, its own piece
look.text: Nehemiah 3 reads like a list. In simple words: The high priest and the priests built the Sheep Gate. Next to them the men of Jericho built. Next to them a goldsmith built. Next to him a maker of perfumes. Shallum and his daughters repaired their section. On and on it goes, gate by gate, all the way around the city.
look.prompt: Why do you think the writer took the time to name so many builders? What does the list say about how the wall got done?

check.q: What was Nehemiah's job in Persia?
check.why: Nehemiah 1 says he was the king's cupbearer, a trusted servant close to the throne.

check.q: What did Nehemiah do on his first night in Jerusalem?
choices: Rode around the broken wall in secret
check.why: Nehemiah 2 says he went out by night to look at the walls before telling anyone his plan.

check.q: How long does Nehemiah 6 say the wall took to finish?
check.why: Nehemiah 6:15 says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

review.q: Which part of the Tanakh holds Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Daniel and Esther?
review.why: These books are in the Ketuvim, the Writings, the third part of the Hebrew Bible.

review.q: Which psalm begins "The LORD is my shepherd"?
review.why: Psalm 23 opens with the shepherd picture. Psalm 100 is a praise psalm and Psalm 137 is a lament.

review.q: What kind of writing is the book of Proverbs?
review.why: Proverbs is a collection of short sayings about living wisely, often in two lines.

review.q: What did Job's friends wrongly claim?
choices: That Job was suffering because he had done wrong
That Job should build an altar
review.why: The friends say only bad people suffer. Job insists he is innocent, and the book does not agree with the friends.

review.q: Why was Daniel thrown to the lions?
choices: He would not bow to a statue
He kept praying when a law forbade it
review.why: Daniel 6 says Daniel kept praying at his window after a law said to pray only to the king.

review.q: What holiday remembers the story of Esther?
review.why: At Purim Jews read the Megillah, the scroll of Esther, and make noise at Haman's name.

review.q: What did Cyrus of Persia do in 538 BCE?
choices: Let the exiles return to Jerusalem
Put Daniel in the lions' den
review.why: Ezra 1 says Cyrus sent out an order letting the people of Judah go home and rebuild.

review.q: Who read the Torah aloud by the Water Gate?
review.why: Nehemiah 8 says Ezra the scribe read the law from morning to midday while helpers explained it.
